name: Chemical depilatory cream

card.summary: Chemical depilatory creams such as Nair and Veet use thioglycolate to dissolve hair at the skin surface, giving a smooth hairless look without a razor.
card.note: Can irritate skin; hair regrows because the follicle is not destroyed.

quick.overview:
A depilatory cream is a lotion or gel that chemically dissolves hair so it can be wiped off. The active ingredient is typically a thiol salt, mostly thioglycolate. It is sold in brands including Nair, Veet and Magic Shave.
For looks, it removes body and face hair with a smooth, razor-free finish, commonly used on legs, arms, chest or back. Because the follicle is not destroyed, hair regrows. Surgical research has also compared it with shaving.
quick.how: The cream is spread on the area for several minutes while it breaks down the hair, then rinsed or wiped away. It comes as creams, gels, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders.
quick.risks: Chemical irritation is the main risk, and product labels advise a patch test and not applying to broken skin. A 2022 laboratory study linked depilatory exposure to acute skin inflammation through a fatty acid binding protein pathway.

lead: Chemical depilatory creams dissolve hair using thiol salts, mainly thioglycolate, which break the disulfide bonds in keratin so the hair can be removed.[1] A typical product contains about 5 to 6 percent calcium thioglycolate in a cream base with alkaline calcium or strontium hydroxide, and hair breaks down in about ten minutes.[1] Because the dermal papilla is not destroyed, hair grows back.[1]

They come as gels, creams, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders, under brands such as Nair, Magic Shave and Veet.[1] Hair-removal ointments go back to Greek and Roman writers, and early sulfide-based products were replaced by thiols because of their odor.[1]

In medical research, depilatory cream has been compared with razor shaving for removing hair before surgery. A 1976 British Medical Journal trial found similar wound infection rates between the two groups, with depilation described as effective, atraumatic and cheaper than shaving.[2] Cochrane reviews of preoperative hair removal have examined these methods.[3]

chain: Thioglycolate breaks down keratin at the surface
Skin looks smooth without razor stubble
angle.text: The cream gives hair-free skin for those who prefer a smooth look on the body or face. Hair regrows, so users repeat it.

infobox: Cream, gel, lotion, aerosol, roll-on, powder

paras: Thiol salts break the disulfide bonds in keratin, and the alkaline pH, held near 12 by calcium or strontium hydroxide, hydrolyzes the hair so it can be rinsed away.[1] Conditioners afterward restore normal skin pH.[1]

Most trials come from surgery. A 1976 controlled trial compared depilatory cream with routine shaving: infection rates were similar, and cream was effective, atraumatic and cheaper, and reduced skin surface bacteria.[2] A 1983 randomized trial compared infection rates after shaving versus depilatory cream,[4] and a 2020 randomized trial in Nigeria tested whether chemical depilation reduces surgical site infection.[5] A 2022 laboratory study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology reported that depilatory-induced skin inflammation depends on epidermal fatty acid binding protein.[6]
Hair-removal threads on forums compare shaving, waxing and creams for the back, chest and legs.
